en: The Sūtra on the Simile of the Moon, Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Dharma-Transmitting Grand Master,
the Purple-Garmented Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove Monastery, together with a community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Just as the bright, full moon seen by the world travels through the void, pure and unimpeded, so too are these bhikṣus:

their majestic deportment remains unimpaired, always like that of a monk with ten years of seniority; endowed with shame and remorse, their bodies and minds are never distracted; entering the homes of laypeople according to the rules of the Dharma, they are likewise pure and untainted."
"O Bhikṣus!

Furthermore, it is like a person with clear vision who, whether entering deep and vast waters, traversing dangerous rivers and streams, or walking upon high and low mountain crags, is able to see everything clearly because of their keen sight, and is thus free from all doubt and fear."
As previously stated, it is the same for the bhikṣus. O bhikṣus!
What I have now spoken is like the moon moving through the sky—pure and unobstructed.
It is like a person with clear vision who, traversing various perils, remains free from all doubt and fear.

Thus, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa does not violate his dignified deportment, always acting as if he were a monk of only one year's standing; endowed with shame and remorse, whether in body or mind, he is never distracted, remaining exactly in accordance with the rules of discipline.
"Entering the homes of laypeople, one remains pure and unstained.
Being free from all timidity and fear is likewise so.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Bhikṣus, when you enter the homes of laypeople, what state of mind should you arouse, and with what appearance should you enter those houses?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The Buddha is the one toward whom we turn; the Buddha is the root of all phenomena; the Buddha is the eye of purity. We do not understand the meaning of this.
We pray that the World-Honored Buddha will skillfully expound it, so that the bhikṣus, having heard it, may fully comprehend it.
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!
Listen attentively and apply your minds well; I shall now speak for you."

If any bhikṣus wish to enter the home of a layperson, they should give rise to a mind that is unattached, unbound, and free from grasping; they should enter that house by relying on the characteristics of ethical discipline. Although they receive offerings and sustenance, they do so solely with the desire to perform meritorious deeds for the sake of others, accepting only according to their own allotted measure.
Furthermore, with skillful attention, one should neither be haughty toward oneself nor disparaging toward others.
Arising such a mind and with such a demeanor, one should enter the house of a layperson.
At that time, the World-Honored One raised his hand and stroked the air, addressing the assembly of bhikṣus:
"What do you think? Does space have any attachment?"
"Is there bondage?
Is there grasping?
The bhikṣus replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“If a bhikṣu enters the house of a layperson with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and free from grasping, it is likewise so.
At that time, the World-Honored One again raised his hand and stroked the air, addressing the assembly of bhikṣus: “O bhikṣus!”
What do you think?
Does space have any attachment?
Is there any bondage?
"Is there any grasping?
The bhikṣus replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!

The Buddha said, “The bhikṣu Kāśyapa is also like this: with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and free from grasping, he enters the homes of laypeople. Although he accepts offerings and sustenance, he does so solely with the desire to perform various meritorious deeds for them, accepting only according to his own allotted measure.”
Furthermore, through skillful attention, one is neither conceited regarding oneself nor disparaging toward others.
Monks! For this reason, one such as the monk Kāśyapa should enter the homes of laypeople and is worthy of receiving offerings.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When bhikṣus preach the Dharma to laypeople, there may be those who are pure and those who are impure; what is the nature of these matters?”
“I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will graciously explain this for us.
The Buddha said, “O Bhikṣus!”
Listen attentively and apply your minds well; I shall now speak for you.

If a bhikṣu, desiring to cause others to give rise to faith and to perform acts of faith by providing them with robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the sick, should preach the Dharma to others for the sake of such benefits, this is not pure.

If a bhikṣu, regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, abides in right view and is free from all defilements—like refined gold from which dross and impurities have been removed—and having seen such a Dharma and realized such a Dharma, he proclaims that Dharma to others just as it was originated by the Buddha; and since this Dharma can bring about freedom from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, once others have heard this Dharma through his teaching, they practice in accordance with it and attain great benefit and happiness throughout the long night. For this reason, he gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth; and by means of this cause, he causes the True Dharma of the Buddha to abide long in the world.
"O Bhikṣus!
If one gives rise to such a mind when preaching the Dharma to others, that is pure.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!"

"You should all know that the bhikṣu Kāśyapa is able to give rise to a pure mind and preach the Dharma to others; because of this purity, he causes the Buddha’s True Dharma to abide long in the world."
Therefore, you bhikṣus, should also train yourselves in this way, according to the principle. Furthermore, bhikṣus,

if there are those who can give rise to such a mind and preach the Dharma for others, I declare them to be supremely pure and true, capable of causing the True Dharma of the Tathāgata to abide long in the world.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra,
the assembly of bhikṣus rejoiced and received it with faith.
The Moon Simile Sutra spoken by the Buddha.
